Tristen Burn - An unnecessary death

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A 13 year old boy dies, after mistreatment and misdiagnosis in our hospitals, a parents plea.

Summary:
Tristen Burn was only 13 years old when he died, a tragedy whatever the circumstances but the fact that the alleged cause of his death was because of a series of errors at two Durban hospitals is for his parents Tim and Vanessa Burn untenable.
In the words of his mother Vanessa: “I would rather be raped 100 times than for my son to have lived through what he did.”
It started with a simple foot injury and Tristen was taken to St Mary’s Hospital in Marionhill, Pinetown. Three days later after a series of misdiagnoses and wrong treatment Tristen was dead.


Further information:
Initially an X Ray was taken and a hairline crack found in one of his foot bones, plaster of paris was cast and the doctor said Tristan would be back at school in two days.
After a night at home in excruciating pain, Tristen went back to St Mary’s the next morning. His foot was X-rayed but the doctor said there was no problem. However, upon Vanessa Burn’s insistence that something was horribly wrong, staff removed the cast.
“When they pulled it off there was a red line where the cast had cut into his leg, although it was not bleeding.
Without checking his blood circulation hospital staff allegedly replaced the cast and sent him home. The parents said they later learnt that if his circulation had been checked, “compartment syndrome”* could have been diagnosed and treated. But his breathing became shallow and he went back to St Mary’s the next day where chest and foot X-rays were taken. He was diagnosed with TB.
“I told them it was impossible for him to have TB because he was a healthy child,” Vanessa said.
He was admitted to the adult TB ward the next morning and his condition deteriorated rapidly. By the afternoon he was feverish, ice cold and gravely gaunt. His back had turned black.
“He was screaming ‘I’m dying, I’m dying. I don’t want to die’,” Vanessa sobbed. Tim said he had to “shout and scream for help” and only then did staff put him on drips and a heart monitor.
Tristen was transferred to RK Khan Hospital where the nightmare continued.
“They didn’t even put on the ambulance sirens because paramedics said it was not a matter of life and death,” Vanessa said.
When they arrived, Burn said he had to help paramedics wheel his son and locate a bed after a nurse said the hospital was full.
“His drips had come out and were dripping all over the place. There was no drip stand so I hung the drips on to a window catch.”
The parents were relieved when a doctor diagnosed Tristen with an acute reaction to the TB medication. Drugs were administered and his pain was relieved.
Burn said that when he returned to see his son in the evening: “The drip had come out, his blood sugar was low and three nurses were standing around him laughing loudly.
“He was lying naked and they had the blanket pulled down. My son was well endowed for a 13-year-old. They said they were trying to give him sugar water. He said he wanted to go to the toilet. I lifted him up on to the bed pan and he was hardly talking to me and just staring as if he could not see me any more,” Burn said, sobbing.
“Then he put his head on my shoulder and I thought he was going to sleep. I didn’t realise he wasn’t breathing until I saw his chest wasn’t moving. I ran to get a nurse and I shouted ‘help me, my son is dying’ and she went off in the other direction. I started giving him mouth to mouth and then staff did CPR.”
A few minutes later Tristan died in the arms of his father, Tim Burn, at RK Khan Hospital.
Independent forensic pathologist Dr Steven Naidoo, who conducted the autopsy, said Tristen did not have TB. “I believe the cause of death was a complication of a too-tight plaster cast placed around the injured limb. He died from septic shock and multiple organ failure from staphylococcal septicaemia, a treatable condition if managed in time.
Tim and Vanessa have spent two years fighting for a proper investigation into this case, at every turn they struck an obstacle. Durban lawyer Ian Dutton is an expert on medical malpractice so much so he has written a book on it. He is shocked by the paralysis and potential failure on a daily basis of both private and public healthcare. The Burn’s case he believes is representative of the shocking state of medical care in South Africa today.
…the Burns have only a 6 months gap left to resolve the case and they are doing it because they want Tristan’s death to be of value to others.

*Compartment syndrome is a serious condition that occurs when there is a large amount of pressure inside a muscle compartment.

Press Release:


Medical Negligence Investigated
Two years have passed since 13-year-old Tristen Burn died in his father’s arms, just three days after treatment in hospital for a minor foot injury. To date, Tristen’s devastated parents have no closure, with little feedback from the hospitals and health professionals involved. Carte Blanche investigates this alleged medical malpractice.


Script:


Tim: We had to wear these masks, I’m just imagining what he’s thinking with us all in these masks, how frightening it must be So I ripped my mask off because I couldn’t speak to him liker that and he said Dad I’m dying they are not listening to me I’m dying…

Link
Vanessa and Tim have vivid memories of their son Tristan it’s been two and a half years since his tragic death. The nightmare started with what seemed to be a trivial incidence

Vanessa: He was running to his best friends place and he hurt his foot. He came to me the next day and said Mom my foot is a bit sore.

Link
By the Monday morning Tristan’s ankle was swollen and painful so Vanessa took him to the nearest hospital St Mary’s in Marion hill, a suburb just outside Durban

V/O 10 sec
St Mary’ s is a state aided district hospital, and for Vanessa and Tim who were not on medical aid it was their only option.

Vanessa: They took him for an X Ray and said there is a green line fracture, and they are going to put the cast on which they did and they just said come back next day for circulation tests and then after 6 weeks we take the cast off.…simple as that.

V/O
Tim and Vanessa are divorced, their children Tristan and Lia spent time with both of them. Tim, a tour guide, was away working when Tristan’s cast was put on.

Tim: He was so excited because he was going to go to school with his cast and he was phoning me and saying what are we going to draw on our cast Dad.

Vanessa: During the evening he started moaning that his leg was sore and he kept me up all night and I couldn’t believe how it could be sore.

Link
The next day Tristan was back at St Mary’s his foot still sore. The Dr says there was no problem he should be back at school in a few days and changed the plaster cast

Vanessa: They were starting to cut the cast and he was screaming, and they were saying but its not sore it cant be sore….

Tim:: and then they told her he is being a baby… so now we are thinking he trying to get out of school.

V/O 7 sec
But what the Dr’s hadn’t picked up was that Tristan had developed a condition known as Compartment Syndrome.

Link
Compartment syndrome is a serious condition where there is a build up of pressure within the muscle tissue possibly the result of plaster cast being too tight

V/O 4 and half sec
Dr Steve Naidoo is an internationally respected forensic pathologist.

Derek: Is the possible cause of Compartment Syndrome a plaster cast that is too tight?
Steve:Well yes certainly it is a well known cause of Compartment Syndrome.
Derek: Is it common or necessary to do a circulation test in the days following the plaster cast being put in place?
Steve: Yes its very typical general practice and orthopaedic principle that a circulation check to be done to make sure plaster cast is not too tight.
Derek When Tristan first went in for treatment they said he would have to come back the next day for a circulation test.
Derek: Was that done?
Vanesa: No,
Derek Then you went home with Tristan?
Vanessa: Yes then we went home and he just lay down and he couldn’t walk and as the night progressed he was breathing very badly he was like …

V/O 8 sec
After a night of virtually no sleep, Vanessa took Tristan back to the hospital… and X Rays were taken of his chest

Vanessa: When they came back the X- Ray’s had blotches on them so the Dr said Mmm he’s got TB and I was like how has he got TB he’s a healthy boy he doesn’t even have a cough… don’t you do a sputum test or a blood test and the Dr just looked at me as if to say don’t undermine my authority

V/O 6 sec
Dr Naidoo attended Tristan’s autopsy, pro bono, on behalf of Vanessa and Tim’
Derek: Dr, were their signs of TB bearing in mind he was being treated for it?
Steve: Well the post mortem was able to confirm that it was not TB what it was, was these multiple seedings or seedlings of septic spots of the lung which on X Ray looks like TB so it wasn’t tuberculosis.

V/O 10 sec
If Compartment syndrome is not treated, the muscle starved of blood and oxygen develops an infection which can spread to the vital organs.

Link
At 9 the next morning Tristan was admitted to the adult TB ward at St Mary’s.

V/O 7 sec
When Tim got to St Mary’s he was met with a scene that left him in total shock’

Tim: They couldn’t take his vital signs they couldn’t take his blood pressure and his sugar level had gone down to virtually zero
Vanessa: He was just lying there I’m still trying to Google TB and the symptoms he was sweating and I had to keep wiping him down, I had to keep running to the kitchen to put ice water to try and cool him down and his body started turning blue bit by bit
Tim: I turned him over and all his back near his kidneys and spine had started to go black and blue.

Link
The St Marys medical team finally admitted there was a major problem and arranged for Tristan to be admitted at the RK Khan Hospital in Chatsworth, but it was a slow and hazardous process

Derek: Vanessa you had been in the ambulance with Tristan?
Vanessa: I was and I said to him why are the sirens not on, it’s not a matter of life and death he said, which even at the time I didn’t realise how serious the situation was.

V/O 5 sec
Tim travelling in his own car arrived at the RK Khan before the ambulance

Tim:. I had to carry my own son out of the ambulance with the ambulance attendant.

LINK
What had started as a minor foot injury had escalated as a race against time to save Tristan’s life although Hospital staff and paramedics didn’t seem to see it that way and here at the RK Khan hospital there was a hardly a sense of urgency

Derek: So at RK Khan they didn’t even know that Tristan was on his way
He was supposed to be put into an ICU ward that what we were told by St Mary’s so they put him in a gen ward.

Tim: We had to bring in another bed no places to hang his drips by now they had three or 4 drips in him, I was holding the drips up myself eventually I had to hang them on the window catches so I could go and help Vanessa look for a Dr to attend to him well eventually the intern came and looked at him saw that it was serious, she then called the DR who was a very nice Dr in fact, we told him about the TB and he said well did they do a sputum test we said no they have not done a sputum test., then he looked again at Tristan and he said I am sure he is having a massive huge reaction to the Tuberculosis medication so he then started pumping Tristan full of steroids and something that made him feel better.. The Dr said to us you’re so lucky your son could have died.

Link
Thinking that Tristan was at last getting the right treatment and even showing signs of recovery Tim left the RK Khan hospital to drop Vanessa at home she hadn’t slept for 4 days words cant describe the scene he came back to.

Tim: As I got back there, their were ¾ nurses around him and they were laughing and joking around him, I just freaked out and I said what’s going on and they said his drips have come out and they were poking trying to look for his veins and the sheets next to him were all full of blood, the puncture marks they were trying to get these drips in

V/O
The nurses left Tim was alone with his son, he lay on the bed next to Tristan

Tim: He looked into my eyes and he put his head down on my chest then I saw that he wasn’t breathing any more and I started giving him mouth to mouth and while I was giving him mouth to mouth Dr came and led me away and they started to give him CPR…5 minutes later they came and told me its too late he’s gone

V/O
Dr Steve Naidoo has his own opinion on why Tristen died’

Steve: The cause of death, I believed, the end result was a state of septic shock and a multiple organ failure. So my opinion about the nature of its development was that a compartment syndrome had developed in its lower limb.

V/O 10 sec
The septic infection had set into the damaged muscle and spread throughout the body, resulting in the organ failure.

Tim: The fact is once autopsy had been done it was only how serious we realised how many mistakes they had made.

V/O 4 sec
The Burns decided to take action and sue for damages

Derek: How often does that happen to people from the townships and people with no money that take their kids to these hospitals and just gets swept under the rug we are not in it for the money we just want people to know someone to take accountability because we feel so guilty in the first place.

Ian Dutton: Sometimes all a patient is looking for is an apology or some sort of sense that a wrong has been addressed. Now the court process is expensive it is time consuming and very often that’s not the way that a person wants to go. But sometimes they are driven to it.

V/O 9 sec
Ian Dutton an advocate in Durban so concerned about the State of our Health Care he’s written a book that address’s the challenges.

Ian Dutton: The medical field is inundated with litigation at the moment the court rolls are becoming increasingly clogged up with this type of sometimes worthy cases and sometimes cases that shouldn’t have been launched in the first place. … And if our Health Care Systems flounders then we all lose out.

V/O 9 sec
St Mary’s and the RK Khan Hospital refused our request for an interview citing that Tristan’s death is still under investigation by the Health Professions Council.

Link
The HPC also refused the opportunity of an interview saying that the case hadn’t been concluded but they did confirm that a complaint had been lodged against 5 drs

V/O 10 sec
A complaint that was lodged two years ago ….
For financial compensation Vanessa and Tim will go to the courts but it’s not about the money.

Derek In this case Ian they could only hope for compensation from pain and suffering
Ian Dutton: In SA the loss of a child through medical negligence or medical malpractice is generally hardly compensated for. If any good can come from this case it’s a highlighting of a situation that is developing in this country. which needs address,

Vanessa: I would just like to say that you have that right to challenge the Dr where I was wrong I trusted the Dr’s, they did not listen to Tristan. We have to live with the guilt because we couldn’t afford medical aid.

Steve: What would have happened if V had not taken Tristan to the hospital
I think there is a good possibility that the inflammation could have settled without a plaster cast and not accelerated into the CB I think it’s quiet possibly T would have survived.
Derek: Be alive today
Steve: Yes…be alive today

Script: Tim: We had to wear these masks, I’m just imagining what he’s thinking with us all in these masks, how frightening it must be So I ripped my mask off because I couldn’t speak to him liker that and he said Dad I’m dying they are not listening to me I’m dying… Link Vanessa and Tim have vivid memories of their son Tristan it’s been two and a half years since his tragic death. The nightmare started with what seemed to be a trivial incidence Vanessa: He was running to his best friends place and he hurt his foot. He came to me the next day and said Mom my foot is a bit sore. Link By the Monday morning Tristan’s ankle was swollen and painful so Vanessa took him to the nearest hospital St Mary’s in Marion hill, a suburb just outside Durban V/O 10 sec St Mary’ s is a state aided district hospital, and for Vanessa and Tim who were not on medical aid it was their only option. Vanessa: They took him for an X Ray and said there is a green line fracture, and they are going to put the cast on which they did and they just said come back next day for circulation tests and then after 6 weeks we take the cast off.…simple as that. V/O Tim and Vanessa are divorced, their children Tristan and Lia spent time with both of them. Tim, a tour guide, was away working when Tristan’s cast was put on. Tim: He was so excited because he was going to go to school with his cast and he was phoning me and saying what are we going to draw on our cast Dad. Vanessa: During the evening he started moaning that his leg was sore and he kept me up all night and I couldn’t believe how it could be sore. Link The next day Tristan was back at St Mary’s his foot still sore. The Dr says there was no problem he should be back at school in a few days and changed the plaster cast Vanessa: They were starting to cut the cast and he was screaming, and they were saying but its not sore it cant be sore…. Tim:: and then they told her he is being a baby… so now we are thinking he trying to get out of school. V/O 7 sec But what the Dr’s hadn’t picked up was that Tristan had developed a condition known as Compartment Syndrome. Link Compartment syndrome is a serious condition where there is a build up of pressure within the muscle tissue possibly the result of plaster cast being too tight V/O 4 and half sec Dr Steve Naidoo is an internationally respected forensic pathologist. Derek: Is the possible cause of Compartment Syndrome a plaster cast that is too tight? Steve:Well yes certainly it is a well known cause of Compartment Syndrome. Derek: Is it common or necessary to do a circulation test in the days following the plaster cast being put in place? Steve: Yes its very typical general practice and orthopaedic principle that a circulation check to be done to make sure plaster cast is not too tight. Derek When Tristan first went in for treatment they said he would have to come back the next day for a circulation test. Derek: Was that done? Vanesa: No, Derek Then you went home with Tristan? Vanessa: Yes then we went home and he just lay down and he couldn’t walk and as the night progressed he was breathing very badly he was like … V/O 8 sec After a night of virtually no sleep, Vanessa took Tristan back to the hospital… and X Rays were taken of his chest Vanessa: When they came back the X- Ray’s had blotches on them so the Dr said Mmm he’s got TB and I was like how has he got TB he’s a healthy boy he doesn’t even have a cough… don’t you do a sputum test or a blood test and the Dr just looked at me as if to say don’t undermine my authority V/O 6 sec Dr Naidoo attended Tristan’s autopsy, pro bono, on behalf of Vanessa and Tim’ Derek: Dr, were their signs of TB bearing in mind he was being treated for it? Steve: Well the post mortem was able to confirm that it was not TB what it was, was these multiple seedings or seedlings of septic spots of the lung which on X Ray looks like TB so it wasn’t tuberculosis. V/O 10 sec If Compartment syndrome is not treated, the muscle starved of blood and oxygen develops an infection which can spread to the vital organs. Link At 9 the next morning Tristan was admitted to the adult TB ward at St Mary’s. V/O 7 sec When Tim got to St Mary’s he was met with a scene that left him in total shock’ Tim: They couldn’t take his vital signs they couldn’t take his blood pressure and his sugar level had gone down to virtually zero Vanessa: He was just lying there I’m still trying to Google TB and the symptoms he was sweating and I had to keep wiping him down, I had to keep running to the kitchen to put ice water to try and cool him down and his body started turning blue bit by bit Tim: I turned him over and all his back near his kidneys and spine had started to go black and blue. Link The St Marys medical team finally admitted there was a major problem and arranged for Tristan to be admitted at the RK Khan Hospital in Chatsworth, but it was a slow and hazardous process Derek: Vanessa you had been in the ambulance with Tristan? Vanessa: I was and I said to him why are the sirens not on, it’s not a matter of life and death he said, which even at the time I didn’t realise how serious the situation was. V/O 5 sec Tim travelling in his own car arrived at the RK Khan before the ambulance Tim:. I had to carry my own son out of the ambulance with the ambulance attendant. LINK What had started as a minor foot injury had escalated as a race against time to save Tristan’s life although Hospital staff and paramedics didn’t seem to see it that way and here at the RK Khan hospital there was a hardly a sense of urgency Derek: So at RK Khan they didn’t even know that Tristan was on his way He was supposed to be put into an ICU ward that what we were told by St Mary’s so they put him in a gen ward. Tim: We had to bring in another bed no places to hang his drips by now they had three or 4 drips in him, I was holding the drips up myself eventually I had to hang them on the window catches so I could go and help Vanessa look for a Dr to attend to him well eventually the intern came and looked at him saw that it was serious, she then called the DR who was a very nice Dr in fact, we told him about the TB and he said well did they do a sputum test we said no they have not done a sputum test., then he looked again at Tristan and he said I am sure he is having a massive huge reaction to the Tuberculosis medication so he then started pumping Tristan full of steroids and something that made him feel better.. The Dr said to us you’re so lucky your son could have died. Link Thinking that Tristan was at last getting the right treatment and even showing signs of recovery Tim left the RK Khan hospital to drop Vanessa at home she hadn’t slept for 4 days words cant describe the scene he came back to. Tim: As I got back there, their were ¾ nurses around him and they were laughing and joking around him, I just freaked out and I said what’s going on and they said his drips have come out and they were poking trying to look for his veins and the sheets next to him were all full of blood, the puncture marks they were trying to get these drips in V/O The nurses left Tim was alone with his son, he lay on the bed next to Tristan Tim: He looked into my eyes and he put his head down on my chest then I saw that he wasn’t breathing any more and I started giving him mouth to mouth and while I was giving him mouth to mouth Dr came and led me away and they started to give him CPR…5 minutes later they came and told me its too late he’s gone V/O Dr Steve Naidoo has his own opinion on why Tristen died’ Steve: The cause of death, I believed, the end result was a state of septic shock and a multiple organ failure. So my opinion about the nature of its development was that a compartment syndrome had developed in its lower limb. V/O 10 sec The septic infection had set into the damaged muscle and spread throughout the body, resulting in the organ failure. Tim: The fact is once autopsy had been done it was only how serious we realised how many mistakes they had made. V/O 4 sec The Burns decided to take action and sue for damages Derek: How often does that happen to people from the townships and people with no money that take their kids to these hospitals and just gets swept under the rug we are not in it for the money we just want people to know someone to take accountability because we feel so guilty in the first place. Ian Dutton: Sometimes all a patient is looking for is an apology or some sort of sense that a wrong has been addressed. Now the court process is expensive it is time consuming and very often that’s not the way that a person wants to go. But sometimes they are driven to it. V/O 9 sec Ian Dutton an advocate in Durban so concerned about the State of our Health Care he’s written a book that address’s the challenges. Ian Dutton: The medical field is inundated with litigation at the moment the court rolls are becoming increasingly clogged up with this type of sometimes worthy cases and sometimes cases that shouldn’t have been launched in the first place. … And if our Health Care Systems flounders then we all lose out. V/O 9 sec St Mary’s and the RK Khan Hospital refused our request for an interview citing that Tristan’s death is still under investigation by the Health Professions Council. Link The HPC also refused the opportunity of an interview saying that the case hadn’t been concluded but they did confirm that a complaint had been lodged against 5 drs V/O 10 sec A complaint that was lodged two years ago …. For financial compensation Vanessa and Tim will go to the courts but it’s not about the money. Derek In this case Ian they could only hope for compensation from pain and suffering Ian Dutton: In SA the loss of a child through medical negligence or medical malpractice is generally hardly compensated for. If any good can come from this case it’s a highlighting of a situation that is developing in this country. which needs address, Vanessa: I would just like to say that you have that right to challenge the Dr where I was wrong I trusted the Dr’s, they did not listen to Tristan. We have to live with the guilt because we couldn’t afford medical aid. Steve: What would have happened if V had not taken Tristan to the hospital I think there is a good possibility that the inflammation could have settled without a plaster cast and not accelerated into the CB I think it’s quiet possibly T would have survived. Derek: Be alive today Steve: Yes…be alive today Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Tristen Burn - An unnecessary death (4424 ) dianajoylucas@hotmail.com 10 November 2014

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A 13 year old boy dies, after mistreatment and misdiagnosis in our hospitals, a parents plea.
metadata.Summary: Tristen Burn was only 13 years old when he died, a tragedy whatever the circumstances but the fact that the alleged cause of his death was because of a series of errors at two Durban hospitals is for his parents Tim and Vanessa Burn untenable. In the words of his mother Vanessa: “I would rather be raped 100 times than for my son to have lived through what he did.” It started with a simple foot injury and Tristen was taken to St Mary’s Hospital in Marionhill, Pinetown. Three days later after a series of misdiagnoses and wrong treatment Tristen was dead.
metadata.Further information: Initially an X Ray was taken and a hairline crack found in one of his foot bones, plaster of paris was cast and the doctor said Tristan would be back at school in two days. After a night at home in excruciating pain, Tristen went back to St Mary’s the next morning. His foot was X-rayed but the doctor said there was no problem. However, upon Vanessa Burn’s insistence that something was horribly wrong, staff removed the cast. “When they pulled it off there was a red line where the cast had cut into his leg, although it was not bleeding. Without checking his blood circulation hospital staff allegedly replaced the cast and sent him home. The parents said they later learnt that if his circulation had been checked, “compartment syndrome”* could have been diagnosed and treated. But his breathing became shallow and he went back to St Mary’s the next day where chest and foot X-rays were taken. He was diagnosed with TB. “I told them it was impossible for him to have TB because he was a healthy child,” Vanessa said. He was admitted to the adult TB ward the next morning and his condition deteriorated rapidly. By the afternoon he was feverish, ice cold and gravely gaunt. His back had turned black. “He was screaming ‘I’m dying, I’m dying. I don’t want to die’,” Vanessa sobbed. Tim said he had to “shout and scream for help” and only then did staff put him on drips and a heart monitor. Tristen was transferred to RK Khan Hospital where the nightmare continued. “They didn’t even put on the ambulance sirens because paramedics said it was not a matter of life and death,” Vanessa said. When they arrived, Burn said he had to help paramedics wheel his son and locate a bed after a nurse said the hospital was full. “His drips had come out and were dripping all over the place. There was no drip stand so I hung the drips on to a window catch.” The parents were relieved when a doctor diagnosed Tristen with an acute reaction to the TB medication. Drugs were administered and his pain was relieved. Burn said that when he returned to see his son in the evening: “The drip had come out, his blood sugar was low and three nurses were standing around him laughing loudly. “He was lying naked and they had the blanket pulled down. My son was well endowed for a 13-year-old. They said they were trying to give him sugar water. He said he wanted to go to the toilet. I lifted him up on to the bed pan and he was hardly talking to me and just staring as if he could not see me any more,” Burn said, sobbing. “Then he put his head on my shoulder and I thought he was going to sleep. I didn’t realise he wasn’t breathing until I saw his chest wasn’t moving. I ran to get a nurse and I shouted ‘help me, my son is dying’ and she went off in the other direction. I started giving him mouth to mouth and then staff did CPR.” A few minutes later Tristan died in the arms of his father, Tim Burn, at RK Khan Hospital. Independent forensic pathologist Dr Steven Naidoo, who conducted the autopsy, said Tristen did not have TB. “I believe the cause of death was a complication of a too-tight plaster cast placed around the injured limb. He died from septic shock and multiple organ failure from staphylococcal septicaemia, a treatable condition if managed in time. Tim and Vanessa have spent two years fighting for a proper investigation into this case, at every turn they struck an obstacle. Durban lawyer Ian Dutton is an expert on medical malpractice so much so he has written a book on it. He is shocked by the paralysis and potential failure on a daily basis of both private and public healthcare. The Burn’s case he believes is representative of the shocking state of medical care in South Africa today. …the Burns have only a 6 months gap left to resolve the case and they are doing it because they want Tristan’s death to be of value to others. *Compartment syndrome is a serious condition that occurs when there is a large amount of pressure inside a muscle compartment.
